passages.text: YELLOW FEVER, a malignant fever of hot climates, so called from the yellow colour which the skin acquires in the course of it.
It is most frequent in the West Indies and in the sea-ports of America, and chiefly attacks strangers lately arrived from colder countries.

The disease begins with chills, violent pains in the head and back, and a flushed face; after a short remission the skin turns yellow, and the patient often throws up a matter like coffee-grounds, called the black vomit, which is commonly a fatal sign.
Its cause is generally ascribed to the putrid exhalations of marshes and of filth, which are raised by the heat of the sun and corrupt the air.

Whether it be contagious is much disputed. Many physicians in Philadelphia, after the great epidemic of 1793, held that it does not pass from one person to another, but arises from the air of the place.
The cure most in favour is by copious bleeding and by calomel given until the mouth becomes sore; others prefer the bark and wine.
It is observed that those who have once recovered from this fever are not attacked by it a second time.
Yellow fever is a viral disease of typically short duration. In most cases, symptoms include fever, chills, loss of appetite, nausea, muscle pains, particularly in the back, and headaches.

In about 15% of people, the disease enters a second, toxic phase after a brief improvement, with recurring fever, jaundice caused by liver damage, and bleeding, including bleeding into the stomach that causes dark vomit. Between 20 and 50% of people who enter this phase die.
The disease is caused by the yellow fever virus and is spread by the bite of an infected female mosquito, mainly Aedes aegypti. It does not spread directly between people.
The virus originated in Africa and reached the Americas with the slave trade in the 17th century. A 1793 epidemic in Philadelphia killed about a tenth of the city's population.
In 1900 a United States Army commission led by Walter Reed confirmed Carlos Finlay's theory that mosquitoes transmit the disease.
A safe and effective vaccine exists, developed by Max Theiler in the 1930s, and one dose protects most people for life. Mosquito control also prevents spread.
No medicine is known to work against the virus itself; treatment consists of supportive care. Survivors have lifelong immunity.

reasons: Same headword in both: YELLOW FEVER and Yellow fever.
Rare terms appear in both: black vomit, Philadelphia, 1793.
The mosquito article scores lower because the 1810 entry never mentions insects.

alignments.label: The yellow skin

britannica.quote: the yellow colour which the skin acquires

alignments.note: Both name the sign that gives the disease its name. Wikipedia adds the cause: the liver is damaged.

alignments.label: Two stages

britannica.quote: after a short remission the skin turns yellow

wikipedia.quote: a second, toxic phase after a brief improvement

alignments.note: The same course of illness: a pause, then the dangerous phase with jaundice.

alignments.label: Black vomit

britannica.quote: called the black vomit, which is commonly a fatal sign

wikipedia.quote: bleeding into the stomach that causes dark vomit

alignments.note: The 1810 entry records the sign. Wikipedia explains it as blood from the stomach.

alignments.label: The cause

britannica.quote: the putrid exhalations of marshes and of filth

wikipedia.quote: caused by the yellow fever virus and is spread by the bite of an infected female mosquito

alignments.note: Bad air from marshes is replaced by a virus carried by mosquitoes. The marshes mattered because mosquitoes breed in water.

alignments.label: Not passed person to person

britannica.quote: it does not pass from one person to another

wikipedia.quote: It does not spread directly between people

alignments.note: Right for the wrong reason. The Philadelphia physicians blamed the local air; the real link between people is the mosquito.

alignments.label: Where it comes from

britannica.quote: most frequent in the West Indies and in the sea-ports of America

wikipedia.quote: The virus originated in Africa and reached the Americas with the slave trade

alignments.note: True of where Britons met it in 1810, but the disease came from Africa.

alignments.label: The cure

britannica.quote: copious bleeding and by calomel given until the mouth becomes sore

alignments.note: Bleeding and mercury (calomel) weakened patients. No drug acts on the virus; care is supportive.

alignments.label: Immunity

britannica.quote: are not attacked by it a second time

alignments.note: The same observation, now with a name for it.

alignments.label: Mosquitoes

wikipedia.quote: confirmed Carlos Finlay's theory that mosquitoes transmit the disease

alignments.note: The mosquito link was proved 90 years after this edition.

alignments.label: Vaccine

wikipedia.quote: A safe and effective vaccine exists

alignments.note: Prevention by vaccine has no counterpart in 1810.

suggestedQuestions: Was the 1810 entry right that yellow fever does not pass from person to person?
What did the 1810 entry think caused yellow fever?
How was yellow fever treated in 1810, and how is it treated now?

Was the 1810 entry right that yellow fev.answer: Yes, but for the wrong reason. The 1810 entry reports that physicians in Philadelphia held that it does not pass from one person to another and arises from the air of the place [B5]. Wikipedia agrees that it does not spread directly between people [W3], but the link is the mosquito, which carries the virus from one person to the next [W3]. The mosquito theory was confirmed in 1900 [W5].

What did the 1810 entry think caused yel.answer:
Putrid exhalations from marshes and filth, raised by the heat of the sun [B4]. Wikipedia names the yellow fever virus, spread by the bite of an infected mosquito [W3].

This is a change in knowledge. The old link to marshes was not empty, since mosquitoes breed in standing water, but that is an inference: neither text says it.

How was yellow fever treated in 1810, an.answer: In 1810 the favoured cure was copious bleeding and calomel, with bark and wine as an alternative [B6]. Today no medicine acts on the virus, so care is supportive [W7], and the disease is prevented with a vaccine and mosquito control [W6].
